brief.intro: New to this project type? A utility-scale solar PV plant is essentially a very large, repeating electrical installation spread across open land — rows of modules on fixed-tilt or tracking racks, wired into strings, converted from DC to AC by inverters, and collected into a substation that connects to the grid. Unlike a building, there is no single 'structure' to build — the programme is driven by procurement of modules, inverters and tracker steel, and by how fast repeatable installation crews can move block by block across the site. Civil works (grading, piling, roads, trenching) happen in parallel across a huge footprint rather than in one sequence, so the real coordination challenge is keeping electrical installation trains fed by civil, not waiting on it. The finish line is not a single test but a grid-code compliance process controlled by the utility, which is often outside the contractor's control and can dominate the tail of the schedule.

scope.name: Site civil & access
scope.desc: Grading, access roads, drainage and security fencing across the plant footprint.

scope.name: Piling & racking/tracker foundations
scope.desc: Driven or screw piles supporting the fixed-tilt or single-axis tracker racking system.

scope.name: Racking / tracker installation
scope.desc: Structural racking or motorised tracker rows that carry the modules.

scope.name: Module installation & DC stringing
scope.desc: PV panels mounted and wired in series into strings, terminated at combiner boxes.

scope.name: Inverters
scope.desc: Central or string inverters (skid-mounted or distributed) converting DC to AC.

scope.name: MV collection network
scope.desc: Underground or overhead medium-voltage cabling gathering power from inverter stations to the substation.

scope.name: Substation & grid interconnection
scope.desc: Step-up transformer, switchgear and the single point of connection to the grid.

scope.name: SCADA / monitoring & controls
scope.desc: Plant SCADA, weather stations and tracker control system.

scope.name: Testing & commissioning
scope.desc: String IV-curve testing, energisation and grid-code compliance verification.

must_get_right: It's procurement and repetition-led — module, inverter and tracker delivery cadence, plus repeatable installation trains, set the pace, not one-off construction.
Civil (piling, roads, trenching) must run ahead of and alongside electrical across a huge footprint — don't let it become a serial dependency.
Grid interconnection and utility approvals are typically the true critical path — track them from day one; they sit outside the contractor's control.
Protect testing windows — string/IV-curve testing scales with panel count, so sequence it block by block behind installation, not as one lump at the end.

basis_of_planning.standard: AACE Recommended Practice 38R-06 — Documenting the Schedule Basis

sections.heading: Scheduling method & tools
sections.body: A Critical Path Method (CPM) network built in Primavera P6, developed to a Level 3 control schedule with retained-logic progress. The install is modelled as repeatable blocks/zones rather than one continuous activity, since piling, racking, stringing and MV collection all progress as parallel installation trains across the site.

sections.heading: Calendars & working time
sections.body: Civil and racking installation run an extended single or two-shift calendar to match the electrical trains' pace; commissioning runs a 7-day calendar toward energisation. A heat/dust-storm allowance is embedded in the civil and installation calendars where applicable.

sections.heading: Sequencing logic & critical path
sections.body: The driving path runs module/inverter/tracker procurement → piling → racking erection → module install & DC stringing → MV collection → substation → grid interconnection & compliance testing. Civil works are not on the critical path once each block's piling is complete and racking can proceed; grid interconnection and utility approval usually govern the finish date.

sections.heading: Key assumptions
sections.body: Land is clear and handed over in workable blocks; geotechnical data confirms the piling method for the whole footprint; a single point of grid interconnection is agreed with the utility; and module/inverter selection is frozen before racking design is finalised. Any change to these invalidates the baseline dates.

sections.heading: Access, resource & site constraints
sections.body: The large footprint supports multiple parallel installation fronts, but crew and equipment mobility between blocks is a real constraint; heavy lifts (transformer) need crane access and clear laydown; installation crews work extended daylight hours and dust/heat control measures apply.

sections.heading: Risks, float & contingency
sections.body: Principal risks: module or inverter delivery slippage, grid interconnection/utility approval delay, and piling refusal in poor ground. Schedule contingency is held before the grid-code compliance test and before COD rather than spread thinly across installation blocks.

sections.heading: Schedule levels of detail
sections.body: Reported at Level 1 (milestones) and Level 2 (summary by block/zone) to the client; controlled at Level 3; expanded to Level 4–5 lookahead for installation trains in the field — consistent with AACE 37R-06.
